Terry -

Thanks for that insight. Looks like you hit the nail on the head as well: I do in fact have negative residuals and standardized parameter estimates over 1, the factors have high reliability, and the correlations among some of the factors are close to 1. That last point is of concern, as it really throws off my theoretical model. I expect high correlations: my indicators are items from separate sections of an assessment, and the factors represent the underlying dimensions of an area of knowledge), therefore I would expect respondents that are strong in one area to be strong in others. But I didn't expect such high correlation - the correlation of the sum of scores for each subsection wasn't this high. And with an assessment that is around 65 items long, I would expect there to be some different dimensions within it.

Given these correlations among the factors are so high, my next thought would be to test a model with only a single factor. This leads me to another question that has been on my mind. I'm using dichotomous indicators, which means I'm using the ordered statement and the estimation uses WLSMV. This means I can't use likelihood-based techniques to choose between the best models. The fit statistics available to me - CFI, TLI, RMSEA - are coming out like the model is essentially perfect, with little difference whether I specify one or many factors.

For example, to test things out (and save processing time), I'm looking at two factors. When treating them as separate, I got CFI=1 and TLI=1.026, with RMSEA=0.000 (pvalue=1.000). The factors correlate perfectly (r=1), calculated by cov2cor(inspect(fit, "coefficients")$psi). When I run the model with only 1 factor (same indicators), I get essentially the same exact fit statistics: CFI=1, TLI=1.024, RMSEA=0.000 (p=1.000). Now I can see how they would fit essentially the same, if the factors are really no different. But I assume under a likelihood-based comparison (say with AIC or BIC) I would see some sort of penalty for the lack of parsimony with 2 factors, which would motivate choosing 1 factor.

It should be clear I'm still mostly a novice in this area, so my bet is that there's something obvious I'm missing, some other way to explain why the factors can be so highly correlated, a mistake I've made which makes them correlate so highly, or some test that can show me that I should run with 1 factor (other than the correlation itself).

Thanks for any counsel.

Robin

Ok. That did not work, since simulataData() did not check if the input
was a parameter table or not (it assumed it was model syntax, called
lavaanify, and we got trouble). I guess you are the first to try this ;-)

This should be fixed in the dev version (0.5-14). But read on.

> library(lavaan)
> set.seed(3141593)
>
> myFLs <- seq(.4, .9, length.out = 6)
> popParams <- c(rep(myFLs, 2), .5)
> N <- 100

>    Y =~ y1 + y2 + y3 + y4 + y5 + y6
>    Y ~ X
> "
> popModel <- lavaanify(myModel)

This is not enough. You probably want:

popModel <- lavaanify(myModel, auto=TRUE, model.type="sem")

to add residuals, etc...

> popModel$ustart <- popParams

This will be slightly more complicated:

popModel$ustart[popModel$op == "=~"] <- rep(c(1, 0.4, 0.5, 0.6, 0.7,
0.8), each=2)
popModel$ustart[popModel$op == "~"] <- 0.5

> popModel$unco <- 0
> popModel$free <- 0

free/unco parameters. And if you must do this, you need to make sure the
entries are integers:

popModel$unco <- 0L
popModel$free <- 0L

> dat <- simulateData(popModel, model.type = "sem", fixed.x = FALSE,
> std.lv <http://std.lv> = TRUE,
>                      return.type = "data.frame", sample.nobs = N,
> standardized = TRUE)

Note that if you use standardized=TRUE, you should not use '1' as the
first factor loadings.

On 06/19/2013 06:22 PM, John Taylor wrote:
> Hi,
>
> I have looked but cannot find (I may have missed it) what default
> constraints Lavaan places upon ordinal CFA models in order to identify
> the model.

The short answer is: the same as Mplus when parameterization=delta.

A formal reference is:

Muth�n, B. (1984). A general structural equation model with dichotomous,
ordered categorical, and continuous latent variable indicators.
Psychometrika, 49(1), 115-132.

but for the multiple-group case, see also:

Muth�n, B., & Christoffersson, A. (1981). Simultaneous factor analysis
of dichotomous variables in several groups. Psychometrika, 46(4), 407-419.

Under the 'delta' parameterization, the residual variances of the
categorical indicators are NOT estimated. They are not fixed to 1 either
(a common misconception), but their values are a function of other
parameter values. The mean of the latent response (y*) is fixed to zero,
while the thresholds are freely estimated.

> categorical indicators are NOT estimated. They are not fixed to 1 either
> (a common misconception), but their values are a function of other
> parameter values. The mean of the latent response (y*) is fixed to zero,
> while the thresholds are freely estimated.
>
> In the multiple-group case, 'scaling factors' are also introduced. By
> default, they are fixed to 1.0 for the first group, but they can be
> freely estimated in the other groups if the thresholds and factor
> loadings are held fixed across groups.

On 06/25/2013 09:14 AM, John Taylor wrote:
> Hi,
>
> While running various ordinal CFA models I noticed that the p-values
> were specified as "(unknown)" and "NA" when ULS was used. I have
> searched through the postings and noticed it was mentioned that ULS is
> not distributed as a chi-square asymptotically and was wondering if that
> was the reason for no p-value calculated or if there is some other reason.

That is the reason indeed. We try to 'avoid' that users report
(unscaled) chi-square test statistics in their papers if estimator="ULS".

> Also, I have seen various references that robust estimation methods like
> ULSMV are appropriate for continuous variables, but are they appropriate
> for ordinal variables? I ask because mainly because I am surprised that
> my models are showing worse fit if I specify the variables as ordinal
> and use a robust method like ULSMV versus if I use ULS. This is
> surprising because my sample size is large (n=1236) and my items are
> univariate normal, though not multivariate normal.

That is an interesting observation. I looked for papers/sources that
could shed some light on this but could not find anything.

Anyone else?

Yves.
